name: Clascoterone

lead: Clascoterone (Winlevi) is a topical antiandrogen cream approved by the FDA in 2020 for acne in patients aged 12 and older, notable as the first new acne drug class in decades. A solution is being investigated for androgenetic alopecia.
Phase 3 trials showed greater lesion reduction than vehicle, and real-world case series report similar results.

paras: It competes with dihydrotestosterone for androgen receptors in sebaceous glands and hair follicles, blocking local androgen signalling without much systemic effect.

Local redness, dryness and itching are most common. Rare, reversible suppression of the adrenal axis was seen under maximal-use conditions, so caution is advised in young patients. It is prescription-only, and its hair-loss use remains investigational.

forums.title: I told you all Clascoterone was the future for skin and hair health

lead: Clascoterone (brand name Winlevi) is a topical androgen receptor inhibitor, a steroid-derived antiandrogen applied to the skin as a 1 percent cream for acne vulgaris [1][2]. The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in August 2020 for patients aged 12 and older, and the agency considers it a first-in-class medicine [1][3]. It was developed by Cassiopea, a spin-out of Cosmo Pharmaceuticals [3].

Two identical phase 3 trials of about 1,440 participants reported that treatment success after 12 weeks was achieved by roughly 18 to 21 percent of clascoterone users versus about 7 to 9 percent on vehicle cream, with greater reductions in lesion counts [1][2][4]. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for topical clascoterone [5]. A higher-strength solution has also been tested for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss) but is not approved for that use [1][6].

The label warns about local irritation, reversible suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, and raised potassium in some trial participants [7]. The European Medicines Agency initially recommended refusal in April 2025 over concerns about adolescents, then granted authorisation in October 2025 after re-examination [1].
infobox: Topical cream (acne); solution under study (hair loss)

paras: Clascoterone 1 percent cream is indicated for acne vulgaris in people 12 and older [7]. It is the first topical therapy aimed at the hormonal component of acne and is not restricted by sex, unlike oral antiandrogens such as spironolactone [2][8][9].

A solution is in development for androgen-dependent scalp hair loss. Wikipedia reports that two phase 3 trials were disclosed in December 2025 with improvements in target-area hair count versus placebo, while absolute changes had not been released at that time [1]. A phase 3 hair-loss trial in 703 participants is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov [10]. Laboratory work found it acts as an androgen receptor antagonist in dermal papilla cells [11]. Small trials are exploring papulopustular rosacea, and a registered study is exploring pilonidal sinus disease; Wikipedia also notes a suggestion for hidradenitis suppurativa [1][12][13][14].

The pivotal programme comprised two identical multicentre, randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase 3 trials (CB-03-01/25 and /26) in people aged 9 and older with moderate or severe facial acne, run from 2015 to 2018 [4]. Participants applied cream twice daily for 12 weeks. Wikipedia reports acne improvement about 8 to 18 percent greater than placebo, and Grokipedia gives treatment success of 18.8 to 20.8 percent versus 6.5 to 8.9 percent [1][2]. Mean reductions in inflammatory lesion counts were 19.4 and 20.0 with clascoterone versus 15.5 and 12.6 with vehicle, according to Grokipedia's summary [2].

An open-label extension of up to nine months in 609 people reported adverse events in 18.1 percent, with nasopharyngitis the most frequent, and a 2023 to 2024 integrated analysis reported short- and long-term efficacy [15][16][17]. An earlier phase 2b dose-escalation study tested 0.1, 0.5 and 1 percent creams [18], and a phase 2a study assessed pharmacokinetics and adrenal suppression [19]. A phase 2 study of the HPA axis response and a 2025 early-phase study on skin irritation and sensitisation have also been published [20][21]. A real-world case series and Canadian experience was published in 2025 [22]. Phase 4 trials on sebum reduction and skin barrier effects are listed as completed or ongoing [23][24][25].

In trials the most common reactions, in 7 to 12 percent of patients, were redness, itching and scaling or dryness, with oedema, stinging and burning at rates similar to vehicle [7]. The label warns of HPA axis suppression, to which paediatric patients may be more susceptible, and of hyperkalaemia [7]. Wikipedia reports HPA suppression in 3 of 42 (7 percent) adolescents and adults tested, normalising within four weeks of stopping, and hyperkalaemia in 5 percent of treated versus 4 percent of placebo participants [1]. The label reports increased malformations in rats and post-implantation loss in rabbits at high subcutaneous doses and no human pregnancy data [7].

The label states that the mechanism in acne is unknown; the drug is believed to compete with dihydrotestosterone at androgen receptors in sebaceous glands and hair follicles [3][7]. In vitro, it inhibited lipid and inflammatory cytokine production in sebocytes [26]. Wikipedia reports minimal systemic absorption, rapid hydrolysis to cortexolone (11-deoxycortisol), and steady state within five days of twice-daily use [1].

Clascoterone is the 17-alpha propionate ester of 11-deoxycortisol, a synthetic pregnane steroid. Esters of this type were found unexpectedly to have antiandrogen activity and clascoterone was selected for development [1]. The FDA approval was based on two trials of 1,440 participants in 99 sites across the US and Europe [1]. Canada, the EU and Brazil have followed, according to Grokipedia, with Sun Pharmaceutical named on the US label and Glenmark marketing in Europe [2][7].

timeline.event: FDA approves Winlevi cream for acne in patients 12 and older [1][3].
AAD guideline gives a conditional recommendation [5].
EMA first recommends refusal (April), then authorises in October after re-examination [1].
Phase 3 hair-loss results for a solution are disclosed in December, per Wikipedia [1].
